display_name: Wind Gap Woodruff Vineyard Pinot Noir, Santa Cruz Mountains
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "The Woodruff Vineyard clings to a steep, south-facing slope in the Santa Cruz Mountains where fractured sandstone and decomposed granite force Pinot Noir roots deep into mineral-rich layers. Minimal intervention winemaking lets high-elevation marine fog and intense afternoon sun dictate a profile that trades plush fruit for sharp, saline tension. Buyers track this wine on curated retail shelves and progressive restaurant lists that value structural transparency over immediate ripeness.",
  "wine_summary": "Wind Gap operates as a site-specific project that tracks cool-climate vineyards struggling under thin topsoil and heavy fog influence. The Woodruff location sits squarely within the AVA’s classic sedimentary geology, where fractured shale and iron-rich sandstone drain rapidly after winter rains and leave vines to fight for water. That stress translates directly to lower yields, thicker skins, and a flavor profile anchored by crushed rock and tart black cherry rather than jammy sweetness. The 2013 and 2014 vintages locked in the region’s signature diurnal shift, preserving bright acidity while building savory depth that rewards bottle age.",
  "terroir_expression": "Perched above the marine fog line, the vineyard wakes up to dense morning moisture that burns off by noon, exposing the canopy to relentless Pacific-cooled sunlight. The shallow, rocky topsoil—dominated by weathered sandstone and ancient seabed shale—holds almost no water, forcing roots to fracture deeper into the substrate. This geological pressure yields grapes with higher acid-to-sugar ratios and pronounced mineral compounds that translate into the wine’s saline lift and grippy, red-fruited core. The steep slope also guarantees constant airflow, stripping away excess humidity that typically breeds dilution in coastal Pinot Noir.",
  "vinification_summary": "Whole-cluster fermentation drives the process, with intact bunches dropped into open-top fermenters to introduce natural stem tannins and lift volatile aromatics without adding oak-derived structure. Cold maceration precedes yeast activity to stabilize color and extract polyphenols from the skins before fermentation begins, building a tannic framework that supports the wine’s lean fruit profile. Native yeasts finish the sugar conversion, preserving the site’s wild herb and iron notes rather than masking them with cultured strains. The result reads like a direct translation of the Woodruff slope, with fermentation choices amplifying site character instead of overriding it.",
  "food_pairing": "Slow-roasted duck confit with a black pepper crust pairs well because the wine’s bright acidity cuts through rich fat while stem-derived tannins bind to rendered lipids, softening the mouthfeel. A wild mushroom and leek tart with Gruyère works as a casual alternative, letting the wine’s earthy, saline character mirror the umami depth of the mushrooms without overwhelming the pastry. Grilled king salmon with miso glaze leans into fine dining territory, where high acid slices through oily fish and crushed-rock minerality complements fermented soy notes. Beef cheek stew with smoked paprika rounds out the options, as the grippy tannins latch onto collagen-rich meat while cool-climate fruit balances spice without clashing.",
  "comparable_wines": "Mount Eden Estate Pinot Noir — shares the same Santa Cruz Mountains elevation and thin, rocky soils, delivering similarly structured, acid-driven Pinot with restrained fruit expression. Littorai Maysara Vineyard Pinot Noir — matches Wind Gap’s whole-cluster philosophy and coastal fog influence, producing wines that prioritize saline tension and earthy complexity over ripe sweetness.",
  "style_profile": "Medium-bodied dry Pinot Noir with firm stem tannins and a saline, crushed-rock finish.",
  "cellar_recommendation": "Drink the 2013 vintage now to catch its peak savory development, while the 2014 still has two to three years of bottle age that will soften the stem tannins and integrate the oak. Store horizontally at 55°F with stable humidity to preserve the high-acid structure.",
  "value_assessment": "Bottles typically trade between $65 and $85, placing it squarely against Mount Eden and Hanzell in the premium cool-climate bracket. At that price, the wine justifies the cost through disciplined tannic structure and site transparency rather than brand prestige. It outperforms similarly priced valley-floor Pinots that rely on ripeness to mask thin texture, making it a strong buy for drinkers who track acid and minerality over plushness.",
  "market_position": "Independent retailers and sommelier-driven restaurant programs stock this wine for its food-friendly structure and transparent sourcing. Collectors of coastal California Pinot seek out specific vintages like 2013 and 2014 for their aging potential, while casual buyers often discover it through curated tasting flights at wine bars that prioritize cool-climate expressions.",
  "insider_take": "Skip this bottle if you expect the plush, dark-fruit profile of Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir. The real tradeoff here is immediate gratification for long-term savory complexity, and that stem-tannic grip will alienate drinkers who prefer soft, unoaked fruit bombs. Buy it only when you want a structural wine that demands a proper meal and rewards patience.",
  "aging_potential_years": 10,
  "drinking_window_min_years": 2,
  "drinking_window_max_years": 12,

  }
}

parsed.wine_summary: Wind Gap operates as a site-specific project that tracks cool-climate vineyards struggling under thin topsoil and heavy fog influence. The Woodruff location sits squarely within the AVA’s classic sedimentary geology, where fractured shale and iron-rich sandstone drain rapidly after winter rains and leave vines to fight for water. That stress translates directly to lower yields, thicker skins, and a flavor profile anchored by crushed rock and tart black cherry rather than jammy sweetness. The 2013 and 2014 vintages locked in the region’s signature diurnal shift, preserving bright acidity while building savory depth that rewards bottle age.
parsed.terroir_expression: Perched above the marine fog line, the vineyard wakes up to dense morning moisture that burns off by noon, exposing the canopy to relentless Pacific-cooled sunlight. The shallow, rocky topsoil—dominated by weathered sandstone and ancient seabed shale—holds almost no water, forcing roots to fracture deeper into the substrate. This geological pressure yields grapes with higher acid-to-sugar ratios and pronounced mineral compounds that translate into the wine’s saline lift and grippy, red-fruited core. The steep slope also guarantees constant airflow, stripping away excess humidity that typically breeds dilution in coastal Pinot Noir.
parsed.vinification_summary: Whole-cluster fermentation drives the process, with intact bunches dropped into open-top fermenters to introduce natural stem tannins and lift volatile aromatics without adding oak-derived structure. Cold maceration precedes yeast activity to stabilize color and extract polyphenols from the skins before fermentation begins, building a tannic framework that supports the wine’s lean fruit profile. Native yeasts finish the sugar conversion, preserving the site’s wild herb and iron notes rather than masking them with cultured strains. The result reads like a direct translation of the Woodruff slope, with fermentation choices amplifying site character instead of overriding it.
parsed.food_pairing: Slow-roasted duck confit with a black pepper crust pairs well because the wine’s bright acidity cuts through rich fat while stem-derived tannins bind to rendered lipids, softening the mouthfeel. A wild mushroom and leek tart with Gruyère works as a casual alternative, letting the wine’s earthy, saline character mirror the umami depth of the mushrooms without overwhelming the pastry. Grilled king salmon with miso glaze leans into fine dining territory, where high acid slices through oily fish and crushed-rock minerality complements fermented soy notes. Beef cheek stew with smoked paprika rounds out the options, as the grippy tannins latch onto collagen-rich meat while cool-climate fruit balances spice without clashing.
parsed.comparable_wines: Mount Eden Estate Pinot Noir — shares the same Santa Cruz Mountains elevation and thin, rocky soils, delivering similarly structured, acid-driven Pinot with restrained fruit expression. Littorai Maysara Vineyard Pinot Noir — matches Wind Gap’s whole-cluster philosophy and coastal fog influence, producing wines that prioritize saline tension and earthy complexity over ripe sweetness.
parsed.style_profile: Medium-bodied dry Pinot Noir with firm stem tannins and a saline, crushed-rock finish.
parsed.cellar_recommendation: Drink the 2013 vintage now to catch its peak savory development, while the 2014 still has two to three years of bottle age that will soften the stem tannins and integrate the oak. Store horizontally at 55°F with stable humidity to preserve the high-acid structure.
parsed.value_assessment: Bottles typically trade between $65 and $85, placing it squarely against Mount Eden and Hanzell in the premium cool-climate bracket. At that price, the wine justifies the cost through disciplined tannic structure and site transparency rather than brand prestige. It outperforms similarly priced valley-floor Pinots that rely on ripeness to mask thin texture, making it a strong buy for drinkers who track acid and minerality over plushness.
parsed.market_position: Independent retailers and sommelier-driven restaurant programs stock this wine for its food-friendly structure and transparent sourcing. Collectors of coastal California Pinot seek out specific vintages like 2013 and 2014 for their aging potential, while casual buyers often discover it through curated tasting flights at wine bars that prioritize cool-climate expressions.
parsed.insider_take: Skip this bottle if you expect the plush, dark-fruit profile of Sonoma Coast Pinot Noir. The real tradeoff here is immediate gratification for long-term savory complexity, and that stem-tannic grip will alienate drinkers who prefer soft, unoaked fruit bombs. Buy it only when you want a structural wine that demands a proper meal and rewards patience.
